events.why: Mexico Against Corruption says Finabien records show 252,901 payments and that the money does not appear in Morena's 2024 campaign filings. Finabien denies acting improperly, and no electoral authority has ruled that the payments were illegal.

reportEvidence.title: #MorenaGate: En la víspera de la elección de 2024, Morena dispersó $134.9 millones en 252,901 apoyos
reportEvidence.dek: Para 2024 se repartieron 134.9 millones de pesos en 252,901 pagos, cerca de 533 pesos por pago. Finabien rechazó cualquier actuación irregular. El monto no aparece en los informes de gastos de campaña.

coverage.title: Investigation finds Morena sent MX$134.9 million through a state financial service in 2024
coverage.summary: Mexico Against Corruption says Finabien records show 252,901 payments and that the money does not appear in Morena's 2024 campaign filings. Finabien denies acting improperly, and no electoral authority has ruled that the payments were illegal.

events.background: Mexico's election agency audits how parties receive and spend money. Its online system is where parties record income and expenses. The documents cited by Mexico Against Corruption show that payments were made. They do not by themselves show why recipients were chosen.
events.view: The MX$134.9 million total covered 252,901 payments, about MX$533 each. The unresolved question is accounting. The investigation says it could not find the amount in Morena's filings, which warrants an official explanation but does not establish vote-buying.
events.prediction: Watch for a response from Morena or the election agency that identifies the account, purpose and reporting category. A clean reconciliation would weaken the concern. An audit finding of unreported spending would strengthen it.

coverage.title: Mexico's farm council challenges preliminary US strawberry duties
coverage.summary: The US Commerce Department's preliminary dumping margin averages 4.83% for winter strawberries from Mexico. A final decision is due January 8, 2027, and Mexico's farm council says the method could extend to other seasonal produce.

events.background: Antidumping cases have two separate tests: the Commerce Department estimates whether imports were sold below fair value, and the US International Trade Commission decides whether the domestic industry was injured. A preliminary margin is not the final result.
events.view: The immediate cost is narrower than the farm council's warning. The case applies to winter strawberries, and the 4.83% average is well below the 18.32% alleged at the start. Any broader precedent depends on the final reasoning, not only the rate.
events.prediction: Watch the Commerce Department's final determination on January 8, followed by the injury decision. Lower or zero final margins would weaken the case. Similar margins and a final injury finding would put the duties on firmer ground.

coverage.title: Screwworm reaches Sonora days before a cattle-export crossing is due to reopen
coverage.summary: Mexico's animal-health agency listed Sonora's first active case in Álamos. The US Agriculture Department has scheduled the Douglas, Arizona, cattle crossing to reopen on August 24, subject to Mexico following the joint control plan.

events.background: New World screwworm larvae feed on living tissue. The US Agriculture Department has tied the border reopening to the joint control plan and inspection of every animal entering through Douglas.
events.view: One confirmed case does not by itself cancel the reopening. Sonora had been one of the northern states kept free of the pest, so the case tests whether the control plan can contain an isolated detection without another trade closure.
events.prediction: Watch the US Agriculture Department's import page and Mexico's animal-health updates before August 24. If the crossing reopens on schedule with the case contained, that would support the control plan. A delay or more northern cases would show the trade risk is rising.

coverage.title: Manufacturing employment edges up 0.1% in June after four monthly declines
coverage.summary: The increase ended a four-month slide, but factory employment remained below a year earlier for a 40th consecutive month. Computer-equipment manufacturing was the exception.

events.background: INEGI's manufacturing survey tracks payroll employment across the factory sector. A 0.1% monthly rise shows that June was better than May, but it does not erase 40 straight months of year-over-year declines.
events.view: The split matters more than the small monthly gain. Factory hiring is still weak across the sector, while computer equipment is growing with demand for data-center hardware. That is a narrow pocket of strength, not a broad manufacturing recovery.
events.prediction: Watch the July survey for another monthly increase and fewer year-over-year losses across industries. If computer equipment remains the main exception, the recovery is still narrow.

events.background: The FAA restored Mexico to Category 1 in September 2023. That status lets Mexican airlines add US routes and codeshares. The latest review tests whether Mexico's regulator still meets international safety-oversight standards.

events.background: Pemex reports quarterly operating and financial data to Mexico's securities regulator. Those filings are the official record for comparing gas production and flaring across periods.
events.view: Compared with a year earlier, flaring nearly doubled. That points to a capture and transport problem: Pemex is producing the gas but cannot use all of it, while Mexico remains dependent on imported US supply.
events.prediction: Watch whether the next Pemex quarterly filing shows lower flaring with steady gas output. That would confirm better capture. Another increase would show the operating constraint remains.

events.background: The regulator's public consultation ended in July, so the 20% cap is still part of draft auction rules, not a completed award. The trade agreement calls for transparent spectrum procedures that promote competition.
events.view: The cap would steer spectrum away from the two national mobile networks and toward smaller industrial-network providers. That may widen participation, but the result depends on whether smaller bidders have enough capital and demand to use the frequencies.
events.prediction: Watch whether the regulator keeps the cap in its final rules and whether qualified smaller bidders enter. Low participation or a legal challenge would expose the tradeoff.

coverage.summary: The Coalition for a Prosperous America has urged US Treasury and US trade office to reject downstream aluminum exemptions for Mexico and Canada in the USMCA review and raise tariffs on fabricated products.

events.background: Section 232 metal tariffs sit outside normal USMCA preferences. During the US trade office's public review, aluminum-industry testimony asked to keep existing tariffs unless Mexico and Canada align their tariffs and enforcement, including for derivative products.
events.view: The latest lobby request is a negotiating position, not a tariff decision. The US trade office has confirmed that steel and aluminum are already part of the bilateral review, so Mexican producers still lack an announced path to relief.
events.prediction: Watch the next official US-Mexico negotiating statement for a specific exemption, quota or enforcement deal. If it contains no measure for aluminum, current tariff treatment remains the best guide. A named exemption or quota would change that.

coverage.title: Mexico's Treasury announces new anti-money-laundering rules effective November 2026
coverage.summary: Mexico's Secretaría de Hacienda has issued modified rules on anti-money-laundering requirements with phased implementation beginning in November 2026.

events.background: The reform amends Mexico's anti-money-laundering law (LFPIORPI), which governs the roughly 120,000 registered individuals and businesses in "vulnerable activities" such as real estate, jewelry and financial services that must report suspicious transactions.
events.view: The shift from a uniform compliance model to a risk-based one lands with a long runway: rules take effect November 30, 2026, main requirements start in 2027, and audits begin only in 2028. That gap matters because Mexico's commercial-bank credit to the private sector is just 35.5% of GDP, so tighter money-laundering oversight targets the formal financial system while informal channels, where 55.2% of workers already operate, remain largely untouched.
events.prediction: Most likely outcome: large firms and financial institutions begin building risk-classification systems well before the 2027 deadline, while smaller registered businesses delay compliance until closer to the 2028 audit start. This would be wrong if Hacienda enforces the November 2026 date more strictly than stated or moves audits earlier.

coverage.summary: Ronald Johnson said the commitments would strengthen security and allow US government activities to resume immediately in phases.

events.background: Michoacán is Mexico's main avocado export state, and US Department of Agriculture inspectors normally certify orchards there before fruit can cross the border, which is why a security-related suspension halts the trade until Washington judges it safe to send staff back. Avocados sit within the broader US-Mexico goods relationship where about 80% of Mexico's exports go to the United States.
events.view: This is a security concession, not a trade agreement, and it addresses federal-state coordination rather than the extortion and cargo theft that INEGI data shows go unreported 93.2% of the time and fall hardest on small producers who cannot pay for protection. The government's claim of a 46% drop in daily homicides since September 2024 is still preliminary prosecutor data, so a security commitment announced this week rests on figures that could be revised once final death certificates arrive.
events.prediction: US personnel most likely resume avocado-related activity in Michoacán in stages over the coming weeks, with no fixed date given. That would be disproven if Washington re-suspends operations following a new violence alert, which is the same trigger that halted the activity this time.

coverage.title: Mexico wins USMCA arbitration against US investment funds over TV Azteca debt
coverage.summary: A USMCA tribunal rejected a 219 million dollar claim by Cyrus and Contrarian funds against Mexico, ruling the investors were not protected by the trade agreement. The decision spares Mexico from paying disputed bondholder claims.

events.background: USMCA contains an investor-state dispute mechanism that lets foreign investors sue a member government before an independent tribunal if they believe treaty protections were violated, separate from Mexico's domestic courts.
events.view: The ruling closes one specific claim rather than settling how USMCA investor protections apply to sovereign debt disputes generally, since it turned on whether these particular bondholders qualified for protection at all. It also matters for public finances: Mexico is already on the last investment-grade rung at Moody's partly because of Pemex support costs, so avoiding a $219 million payout keeps one more claim off a debt load that rose to 53.2% of GDP in 2025.
events.prediction: The funds are likely to explore appeal routes or alternative legal claims rather than drop the matter, since $219 million is a large sum to abandon after losing on jurisdiction rather than merits. That view would be wrong if Cyrus and Contrarian publicly confirm they are not pursuing further action.

coverage.title: House Republicans back US trade office strategy to delay US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement review
coverage.summary: A coalition of 167 House Republicans formally endorsed the US Trade Representative's decision to extend the joint review of the USMCA, delaying the agreement's renewal timeline beyond its scheduled completion date.

events.background: Under Article 34.7 of the USMCA, the first joint review took place on 1 July 2026 and the US Trade Representative can extend that review process rather than accept the treaty's default 16-year renewal, keeping the pact's future rules unsettled year to year.
events.view: This letter is a signal, not a policy change: 167 House Republicans are backing an extended review, but the review already reverted to annual cycles after the US declined the 16-year extension on 1 July, so the practical trading rules for existing Mexican factories do not shift yet. The people affected are exporters weighing new, long-payback plants, since about 80% of Mexico's exports already depend on the US market and any delay just prolongs the uncertainty they face on future rules of origin.
events.prediction: The joint review process likely continues on its annual track without a firm renewal date, since Congress has no binding vote here, only influence over the Trade Representative's negotiating posture. That would be wrong if Greer's office sets a concrete new review deadline or Mexico and Canada agree to specific concessions this year.

coverage.title: Sheinbaum says Sinaloa's interim governor should serve through October 2027
coverage.summary: Sinaloa's Congress is due to name a replacement Monday after granting Rubén Rocha Moya a second indefinite leave.

coverage.title: Mexican governor indicted by US seeks leave again after contentious return to office
coverage.summary: Rocha sought a second indefinite leave about a day and a half after returning to office.

events.background: Sinaloa's constitution requires Congress to appoint an interim governor when an absence lasts more than 30 days. The appointment requires an absolute majority.
events.view: The second leave turns a brief return into a longer succession decision. If Congress appoints someone through October 2027, that person, not Rocha, will run the state while the US case proceeds.
events.prediction: Congress's appointment will show whether the handover lasts through October 2027. A shorter term would leave the succession open.
